title: Finding a starting point in the three collections
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: The three collections provide different starting points for a conversation: collectible design, memory art and personal art.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: The three collections provide different starting points for a conversation: collectible design, memory art and personal art. Begin with the purpose of the request rather than trying to classify every possible object perfectly.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Browse the collection closest to your intention and note which features interest you. If the idea crosses collections, describe that in the custom brief. Keep a short reference list instead of assuming a collection label determines feasibility. Use the current collection pages to check what is actually shown.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A keepsake intended as a gift may connect memory art and personal art. The brief can explain both meanings without creating two separate requests for the same idea.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Does the idea need a custom brief?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Browsing or saving a piece does not reserve it or confirm a quotation. The conversation and final agreement remain separate.

sections.heading: Choose the next question
paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Using a search term when you do not know the product name
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: Search works best as an iterative way to find references.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Search works best as an iterative way to find references. If you do not know a product name, begin with a visible form, intended use or topic you can describe.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Try a short term, inspect the result types and refine it if needed. Compare the result title and description before opening it. If an exact phrase returns little, try a simpler word. Record useful page links so the later brief identifies the reference precisely.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A search for a table-related form may reveal both pieces and reading. Those results serve different purposes: one shows a catalogue reference, another helps prepare the discussion.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What ordinary word describes the idea?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: A search result is not confirmation of stock, suitability or an agreed service. Read the actual page and current policy where relevant.

title: Reading applied filter chips
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: Applied filter chips show the choices currently narrowing a list.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Applied filter chips show the choices currently narrowing a list. Reading them before changing the search can explain why an expected result is missing.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Look at each active chip and compare it with your intended search. Remove one restrictive choice at a time where the interface offers that control. Use Clear filters when you want a fresh view. Check the resulting list rather than assuming a filter promises a particular number of entries.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A narrow topic and journey combination may leave few results even when either category alone has more. Removing one choice helps identify the restriction.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes

checklist: Did clearing it reveal a useful reference?

paragraphs: Filters describe available indexed content. They do not create records, confirm product suitability or substitute for a direct inquiry.

title: Preparing a shortlist for a later conversation
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: A shortlist is most useful when every saved reference has a reason.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A shortlist is most useful when every saved reference has a reason. Saving many pieces without notes can make the later conversation less focused.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Choose a small set and record the feature that matters for each: outline, colour relationship, use or a question. Keep conflicting alternatives labelled. Review the list before beginning a brief so superseded ideas do not look equally current. Retain the page links alongside your notes.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: One saved piece may explain a preferred edge while another explains a room relationship. Neither necessarily represents a request to reproduce the complete object.

title: A one-page index linking a saved reference to later decisions
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: A one-page reference index connects images to decisions over time.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A one-page reference index connects images to decisions over time. It prevents the same image from acquiring a different meaning in every message.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Give each reference a short code, page link and purpose. Add the date first used and the decision it informed. Keep a status column for current, alternative or superseded. When a proposal arrives, link its version to the relevant reference rather than replacing the reference's original meaning.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: Reference R2 might concern edge shape only. A later proposal can respond to R2 without implying that its colour or dimensions were also requested.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: The index is a personal discussion aid. It does not turn an inspiration image into an approved design or material specification.

title: Keeping a receipt reference easy to find
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: An inquiry reference helps the atelier locate a saved request.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: An inquiry reference helps the atelier locate a saved request. Keep it somewhere you can find without relying on the continued availability of a private receipt link.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: After a successful save, note the RLA reference and the date in your own records. Keep the reviewed summary where appropriate for your privacy needs. Use that reference when contacting the atelier about the same request. Avoid creating another inquiry solely to recover an existing one.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A receipt link and an inquiry reference are different. The private receipt access can expire while the saved inquiry remains available to the studio.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Can it be distinguished from a proposal version?
What information will help identify the existing inquiry?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Current receipt access lasts up to 24 hours in the original browser. The website cannot confirm that a prepared WhatsApp message was sent.

title: What Open WhatsApp and Copy each do
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: Open WhatsApp and Copy are two ways to use a saved summary.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: Open WhatsApp and Copy are two ways to use a saved summary. Neither means the website has sent the message on your behalf.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Review the saved details first. Open WhatsApp can take you toward the conversation; Copy places the summary on the clipboard for pasting. Check the destination and pasted content before pressing Send yourself. A long brief may need copying rather than relying on a prefilled link.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: If WhatsApp opens without the full expected text, use the saved receipt's Copy option and inspect the pasted result. Do not create another inquiry just to send the same details.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Have you deliberately sent the reviewed message?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: The website cannot verify whether you pressed Send or whether the recipient read the message. A saved request is not a confirmed order.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Returning to an unfinished form safely
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: An unfinished form and a saved inquiry are different states.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: An unfinished form and a saved inquiry are different states. Before leaving a form, keep your important wording somewhere private that you control rather than assuming the website will recover every unsaved field.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: If returning to an open form, review each field and reference before submitting. Look for a successful-save receipt before starting again. If a receipt already exists, use its reference for follow-up. Avoid relying on the browser's Back button as proof that a submission did or did not succeed.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A form still visible after an interruption may contain text without a confirmed save. Conversely, a saved inquiry may exist even if the message handoff was interrupted.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: Is this an unfinished draft or an existing inquiry?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: Do not assume unsaved form recovery or cross-device synchronization. Ask for help using the existing reference when a save is confirmed.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Recognising an error without submitting twice
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: A failed action needs a careful reading of the visible result.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: A failed action needs a careful reading of the visible result. Repeating a submission immediately can create confusion about which attempt succeeded.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Read the error message and check whether a receipt or inquiry reference appeared. Correct a clearly identified field issue before retrying. If the outcome is uncertain, retain the visible details and contact the atelier rather than repeatedly submitting. Never include private access tokens in a public support message.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A message-handoff problem after a successful save is different from a failed save. The existing receipt can be used to copy or reopen the message without creating another request.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What can be checked before another submission?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: This guidance does not guarantee recovery from every network failure. The important distinction is whether a saved reference exists.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.

title: Checking the language of your saved request
eyebrow: Using the website and saved requests
description: The language used to browse the site and the meaning of a saved request both deserve review.

sections.heading: The question behind the worksheet
paragraphs: The language used to browse the site and the meaning of a saved request both deserve review. A translated interface does not remove the need to inspect names, dates and the actual summary.

sections.heading: Work through the observation
paragraphs: Read the saved summary in the language and script it contains. Compare exact personalization text against your source. If a page falls back to English, do not assume an unseen translation has been approved. Keep any requested language correction separate from a design change.

sections.heading: A worked example to compare
paragraphs: A name entered in one script should be compared character by character after copying the summary into another application. Interface labels do not verify that text.

sections.heading: Questions to put in your notes
paragraphs: Use these prompts to produce a short record you can revisit. Date the sheet, identify the reference you used and leave unknowns explicitly unanswered. Keep site facts, personal preferences and requests for confirmation separate.
checklist: What language does the summary contain?
Which wording needs a fluent reader's check?

sections.heading: What this exercise cannot establish
paragraphs: English fallback is explicit where reviewed translations are absent. Native-language accuracy needs an actual qualified reader, not an automated status assumption.

paragraphs: Keep the resulting note with your current brief. Before sending it, check that it explains one decision clearly and does not turn a preference into an agreed detail. Use the current linked page for the relevant website guidance, and bring any piece-specific uncertainty to the atelier.
